warmup.q: You move api.issuer.example to a new IP address at 10:00. Before the change its record had a TTL of 3600 seconds. A payment service resolved the name at 09:59 through the company's resolver, with the JDK's default settings. At the latest, when does a new connection from that service go to the new address?
options: At once: the authoritative server pushes the change to every resolver
At about 11:00, when the resolver's copy expires, give or take the JVM's own 30-second cache
warmup.why: Nothing pushes DNS changes. The resolver copied the old answer at 09:59 and may hand it out until its TTL runs out around 10:59, and the JVM may keep its own copy up to 30 seconds longer. "Propagation" is only caches expiring at different times, and a TTL of 3600 means one hour, not two days. A pooled connection opened earlier keeps talking to the old address until the pool closes it, whatever DNS says.

sections.h: A name is a path in a tree, and each part has an owner
sections.html:
example.com isn't a key in one big table. Nobody could run that table: hundreds of millions of names, changed by their owners every minute, asked for billions of times an hour. DNS, the Domain Name System, splits the problem the way the names are split: at the dots.

Read a name from the right. api.pay.example.com. ends in an invisible dot, the root. Under the root are the top-level domains (TLDs): com, org, uk, test. Under com is example, and under that whatever its owner adds. Any node of the tree can be cut off and handed to a different owner, together with everything below it. That piece is a zone, and handing it over is a delegation. The root zone is a short list saying who runs each TLD. The com zone says who runs each of its hundred-odd million names, and nothing else about them. The example.com zone holds the actual addresses of example.com and its children. Each zone is served by its authoritative servers, the only servers whose answers about that zone are originals rather than copies.

DNS stores everything as resource records: a name, a type, a TTL (how many seconds anyone may keep a copy) and data. These types cover most of what you'll meet, with real records from this lesson's Try its:

Type Holds Example
A an IPv4 address example.com. 300 A 104.20.23.154
AAAA an IPv6 address (lesson 5) example.com. AAAA 2606:4700:10::6814:179a
CNAME "this name is an alias of that one" www.wikipedia.org. CNAME dyna.wikimedia.org.
NS the servers of a zone: a delegation example.com. NS hera.ns.cloudflare.com.
SOA facts about a zone, among them how long to remember a "no" iana.org. SOA sns.dns.icann.org. ... 3600
MX, TXT mail servers, free text example.com. TXT "v=spf1 -all"

A delegation is just NS records in the parent zone. So to find example.com's address you start at the root, which only knows who runs com; ask com, which only knows who runs example.com; then ask that, which knows the answer. Three questions, each to a different organisation. Only the zone's owner can change its records, and nobody else has to be told when it does.

The root itself is served under 13 names, a.root-servers.net to m.root-servers.net. Each name is many machines around the world sharing one address (anycast, from lesson 4's Go deeper), more than a thousand machines in all, so a root server is never far away. Their addresses are built into resolver software, because nothing can be looked up before them. The next section follows one lookup down this tree.

sections.h: A recursive resolver walks the tree for you
sections.html:
Your program never walks the tree itself. Three kinds of DNS software share the work.

The stub resolver lives inside your process. On Linux it is part of the C library: getaddrinfo(), which the JVM calls for InetAddress.getByName. It reads /etc/hosts first, then /etc/resolv.conf for the address of one recursive resolver. It sends that resolver one question with the RD flag set (recursion desired: "do the whole job for me") and waits for the final answer. It caches nothing itself. In the lab box /etc/resolv.conf says nameserver 127.0.0.11, Docker's built-in resolver. On a laptop it is usually the home router, the company's resolver or a public one such as 1.1.1.1.

The recursive resolver does the walking. It sends iterative queries: questions without RD, which every server answers with what it knows, either the answer or a referral, "I don't know, but these servers do". It starts at a root server. The root answers example.com A? with a referral to the 13 com servers in the authority section, plus their addresses in the additional section. Those addresses are called glue: without them the resolver would have to look up a.gtld-servers.net before it could ask it anything. The com server refers it on to example.com's two Cloudflare servers, and one of those answers with the A records and the AA (authoritative answer) flag. The resolver hands the records to the stub with RA (recursion available) set and AA clear, because it is passing on a copy.

Then it keeps everything it learned. The referrals had TTLs of 172,800 seconds, two days, so for two days this resolver goes straight to the com servers and to Cloudflare, and asks the root nothing. The A records had a TTL of 300, so for 5 minutes it answers example.com from memory without asking anyone. On a busy resolver almost every lookup is a cache hit.

All of this travels as UDP datagrams to port 53, as lesson 6 showed: one question, one answer, resent after a timeout. An answer too big for one datagram comes back with the TC (truncated) flag, and the resolver asks again over TCP.

steps: Start the lab box from the labs folder: docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box.

video.title: How a DNS lookup walks the tree

sections.h: A DNS message: a 12-byte header, the question, and records
sections.html:
Every DNS message, question or answer, has the same shape, defined in RFC 1035 in 1987 and still read by every resolver. This is the whole query dig sent for example.com in the Try it below, 29 bytes:

9984 0100 0001 0000 0000 0000   07 6578616d706c65 03 636f6d 00   0001 0001
header (12 bytes)               e x a m p l e      c o m   end     A    IN

The first 12 bytes are the header, six 16-bit numbers. 9984 is the ID, 39300, picked at random by dig. The answer must carry the same ID, which is how a client over UDP matches answers to questions (lesson 6). 0100 holds the flags; only RD is set. Then four counts: one question, no answers, no authority records, no additional records.

The question is a name, a type and a class. The name travels as labels, each a length byte and then that many characters: 07 example 03 com 00. No dots go on the wire, the final zero is the root, and a label can't be longer than 63 bytes. Type 0001 is A; class 0001 is IN, the internet.

The answer from 1.1.1.1 starts with the same ID, flags 8180 (QR: this is a response; RD copied back; RA: recursion available) and counts of one question and two answers. It repeats the question, then gives each answer record as a name, a type (16 bits), a class (16), a TTL (32 bits, in seconds), a data length (16) and the data. An A record's data is the 4-byte address: ac42 93f3 is 172.66.147.243.

Each answer's name is only two bytes: c0 0c. A length byte with its top two bits set is not a length but a pointer. The other 14 bits are an offset from the start of the message, here 12, where the question's name begins. This is name compression: the same names repeat all over an answer, and a pointer can replace any ending of a name that appeared earlier. In the CNAME answer the lab reads, dyna.wikimedia.org is written as 04 dyna 09 wikimedia followed by a pointer to the org inside the question, and the next record's name is a pointer to that. Compression kept answers inside 512 bytes, the old limit for DNS over UDP.

It also makes parsing a security matter. A parser that follows pointers blindly loops forever on a pointer that points to itself, and real DNS software has shipped that bug. The lab's parser follows only pointers that point backwards.

try.title: Capture a lookup and find the fields
steps: In the lab box, capture one lookup against 1.1.1.1. +noedns and +noadflag switch off two later additions (an extra record that announces support for bigger answers, and a DNSSEC flag), so the bytes are exactly the 1987 format. This capture is the lab's test input.

In the hex, the DNS message starts at byte 42 (0x2a): 14 bytes of Ethernet, 20 of IP and 8 of UDP come first. Find the ID in both frames and check they match. Then find the flags, the four counts, the two c00c pointers, the TTLs and the addresses.
Predict before you look: how many bytes is the answer, if the query is 29 bytes and each A record takes a 2-byte pointer, 10 bytes of fields and 4 of address?

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: tcpdump -i eth0 -nn --immediate-mode -w /tmp/dns.pcap 'udp port 53' 2>/dev/null & sleep 1 dig +noedns +noadflag @1.1.1.1 example.com A sleep 1; kill %1; wait tcpdump -r /tmp/dns.pcap -nn -XX

	0x0000:  66c8 1e81 add7 fa2e d3f4 88ee 0800 4500  f.............E.
	0x0010:  0059 c686 0000 3611 0ff6 0101 0101 ac14  .Y....6.........

The ID 9984 (39300) sits at 0x2a in both frames; tcpdump's 39300+ means "ID 39300, RD set". The answer is 29 + 16 + 16 = 61 bytes, tcpdump's (61). Each record starts with c00c and carries TTL 0000 001e, 30 seconds. 1.1.1.1 hands out its copy of example.com with a TTL of 30 even though the authoritative server says 300, which a resolver is allowed to do: it may keep a copy for less time than the TTL, never longer. Your ID, port and TTL will differ.

sections.h: Every answer is a copy with an expiry date
sections.html:
A resolver that passes an answer on keeps a copy for as long as the TTL allows, and tells the next client only the time that is left. Ask a busy resolver twice, 16 seconds apart, and the TTL in the answer drops by 16. That one rule explains most DNS surprises in production.

Nothing is pushed. When the owner of ledger.pay.test changes its address, the authoritative server answers with the new one at once, and every copy already sitting in a cache stays wrong until its own TTL runs out. Different resolvers fetched their copies at different moments, so the world switches over gradually during one TTL. That spread is all that "DNS propagation" is. With a TTL of 300 it is over in 5 minutes; with 86,400 it takes a day, which is where the "24 to 48 hours" folklore comes from. So plan a migration one TTL ahead: lower the TTL to 60 a day before (the old, long TTL has to expire everywhere first), move, then raise it again.

"No" is cached too. If a name doesn't exist, the authoritative server answers NXDOMAIN (response code 3) and puts its zone's SOA record in the authority section. RFC 2308 says to cache that "no" for the smaller of the SOA record's own TTL and the SOA's minimum field, its last number. For pay.test both are 60 seconds; for iana.org, 3600. The trap: a deploy script that looks a name up a few seconds before the record is created caches the NXDOMAIN, and the new service stays unreachable through that resolver for up to that long after the record exists. A name that exists but has no record of the asked type gets NOERROR with no answers, cached the same way.

The resolver's side of this is a few lines: store each answer with "expires at now + TTL", serve it while now is earlier, and report expiry minus now as the TTL. A CNAME chain is only as fresh as its shortest link: in the Wikipedia answer the lab reads, the CNAME had a day left and the A record 2 seconds, so the whole answer expires in 2. The lab builds this cache.

The Try it below runs an authoritative server for the made-up zone pay.test on router and a caching resolver on peer, about 200 lines of Python in labs/env/net/dns.py (the lab box image has no DNS server software). You change a record at the source and watch the resolver keep the old one until its TTL is up.

try.title: Change a record and watch the cache keep the old one
steps: From the labs folder, with the lab network up (docker compose -f env/net.yml up -d), start the authoritative server on router (it serves a copy of env/net/pay.test.zone from /tmp) and the caching resolver on peer. The c function runs a command on client; it works in zsh and bash.
Ask the resolver for ledger.pay.test, then move ledger to 10.10.4.41 at the source. Predict what the resolver says right after the change, and when it will first say .41.
Ask for a name that doesn't exist, then read the resolver's log on peer. Both servers stop with docker compose -f env/net.yml down.

code.title: in labs/
code.html: docker compose -f env/net.yml exec -d router python3 /labs/env/net/dns.py auth 10.10.1.2 /labs/env/net/pay.test.zone docker compose -f env/net.yml exec -d peer python3 /labs/env/net/dns.py resolver 10.10.1.20 10.10.1.2 c() { docker compose -f env/net.yml exec client "$@"; } c dig @10.10.1.20 ledger.pay.test +noall +answer docker compose -f env/net.yml exec router sed -i 's/10.10.4.40/10.10.4.41/' /tmp/pay.test.zone c dig @10.10.1.2 ledger.pay.test +norecurse +noall +answer c dig @10.10.1.20 ledger.pay.test +noall +answer sleep 15; c dig @10.10.1.20 ledger.pay.test +noall +answer sleep 15; c dig @10.10.1.20 ledger.pay.test +noall +answer c dig @10.10.1.20 refund.pay.test | grep -E 'status|SOA' docker compose -f env/net.yml exec peer cat /tmp/resolver.log

ledger.pay.test.	30	IN	A	10.10.4.41
ledger.pay.test.	28	IN	A	10.10.4.40
ledger.pay.test.	12	IN	A	10.10.4.40

;; ->>HEADER<<- opcode: QUERY, status: NXDOMAIN, id: 29576
pay.test.		60	IN	SOA	ns.pay.test. hostmaster.pay.test. 1 7200 3600 1209600 60
20:17:35 ledger.pay.test. cache miss, asked 10.10.1.2, keeping it 30 s
20:17:36 ledger.pay.test. cache hit, 28 s left
20:17:52 ledger.pay.test. cache hit, 12 s left

Right after the change the authority (@10.10.1.2) already said .41, while the resolver kept answering .40 with its TTL counting down, 28 and then 12. Only once its copy expired did it ask again and pick up .41. Nobody told it about the change, and nobody needed to. The missing name got NXDOMAIN with the zone's SOA, and the resolver keeps that "no" for 60 seconds: the SOA record's TTL and its minimum field, the last number, are both 60.

sections.h: The JVM keeps its own copy, and so does your connection pool
sections.html:
The resolver's cache is not the last one. Between DNS and your payment request sit two more, and neither reads the TTL.

The JVM caches the result of every successful lookup in InetAddress for 30 seconds by default, whatever TTL the answer had, and every failed one for 10 seconds. The settings are the security properties networkaddress.cache.ttl and networkaddress.cache.negative.ttl. Set them in $JAVA_HOME/conf/security/java.security, or with Security.setProperty at startup before the first lookup; -Dsun.net.inetaddr.ttl sets the first from the command line. 0 turns the cache off and -1 keeps answers forever. Thirty seconds is a sensible default: a record with a TTL of 5 still costs at most one lookup per 30 seconds per JVM, and a changed record is picked up at most 30 seconds late.

The connection pool is the bigger one. DNS is consulted only when a connection opens. A pooled HTTP connection to api.issuer.example opened at 09:00 keeps going to the address resolved at 09:00 for as long as the pool keeps it, whatever DNS says by now. When a provider moves its API to a new address and keeps the old one running for a while, your service follows only as its pool replaces connections. That is why HTTP clients have a maximum connection lifetime, and why the old address finally refusing connections is often what moves you.

Linux itself adds no cache: glibc's stub asks the resolver every time, unless the host runs a local cache such as systemd-resolved or nscd. macOS does cache, in mDNSResponder.

try.title: Watch the JVM hold on to an old address
steps: In the lab box, add ledger.pay.test to /etc/hosts, the first place the stub resolver looks. The move function rewrites the file in place: Docker mounts /etc/hosts into the container, so sed -i can't replace it.
Schedule a move to .41 in 10 seconds, and run JvmCache.java, which resolves the name once a second for 40 seconds and prints a line whenever the answer changes. Predict when the JVM sees .41.
Move it back and run again with -Dsun.net.inetaddr.ttl=0, which turns the JVM's cache off.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: echo '10.10.4.40 ledger.pay.test' >> /etc/hosts move() { sed "s/$1/$2/" /etc/hosts > /tmp/h; cat /tmp/h > /etc/hosts; echo "$(date +%T) /etc/hosts now says $2"; } (sleep 10; move 10.10.4.40 10.10.4.41) & java /labs/net/src/demo/java/sfz/net/l09/demo/JvmCache.java ledger.pay.test 40 move 10.10.4.41 10.10.4.40 (sleep 10; move 10.10.4.40 10.10.4.41) & java -Dsun.net.inetaddr.ttl=0 /labs/net/src/demo/java/sfz/net/l09/demo/JvmCache.java ledger.pay.test 15

try.expect:
From one run:

networkaddress.cache.ttl = null, sun.net.inetaddr.ttl = null
20:50:22  t= 0 s  ledger.pay.test -> 10.10.4.40
20:50:30  /etc/hosts now says 10.10.4.41
20:50:53  t=30 s  ledger.pay.test -> 10.10.4.41
done after 40 s
20:51:04  /etc/hosts now says 10.10.4.40
networkaddress.cache.ttl = null, sun.net.inetaddr.ttl = 0
20:51:06  t= 0 s  ledger.pay.test -> 10.10.4.40
20:51:14  /etc/hosts now says 10.10.4.41
20:51:14  t= 8 s  ledger.pay.test -> 10.10.4.41
done after 15 s

The file changed 8 seconds into the first run (the JVM took about 2 of the 10 seconds to start), and the JVM kept answering .40 until its 30-second entry expired, 22 seconds after the change. With the cache off it saw the change within the second. null means the property isn't set, so the JDK's built-in 30 seconds applies. A hosts file has no TTL at all, which makes the JVM's own rule easy to see. If the JVM starts slowly on your machine and the first line already says .41, run it again.

analogy: DNS works like reception desks in a city of office towers. The city's front desk (the root) doesn't know anyone's phone number, only which building each company is in. The building's lobby desk (the TLD) knows which floor a company is on. The company's own receptionist (the authoritative server) knows the extension. Your assistant (the recursive resolver) does this walk for you and writes every answer on a sticky note with an expiry time, so next week she skips the city desk and goes straight to the building. The analogy breaks on updates: in a real office someone would phone your assistant when a number changed. In DNS nobody ever does. The sticky note is trusted until it expires, and your own address book (the JVM) and speed-dial buttons (a connection pool) keep their own copies by their own rules.
world: DNS sits under every outbound call your payment services make, and its caches decide how fast you follow a change. When a card issuer fails over by pointing api.issuer.example at its second data centre, your Quarkus service follows only after the company resolver's copy expires (the record's TTL), plus up to 30 seconds of the JVM's cache, and pooled connections keep using the old address until the pool replaces them, so set a maximum connection lifetime that fits your failover target. Negative caching bites during deploys: a Temporal worker or a Kafka client that starts before its new service's DNS record exists caches the NXDOMAIN, 10 seconds in the JVM and up to the SOA minimum in the resolver, and fails for that long after the record appears. And because lookups use UDP with a 5-second retry in glibc, one lost DNS packet adds 5 seconds to the first call after the JVM's cache expires, which looks like a slow issuer in your traces.
mistake: The common mistake is changing a record and lowering its TTL in the same step, then wondering why clients follow slowly. Every resolver that cached the old record did so under the old TTL, say 86,400 seconds, and will keep its copy for up to a day whatever the new record says. People read that as "DNS propagation takes 24 to 48 hours" and wait it out. Lower the TTL first, wait at least one old TTL so every cached copy has been replaced by one carrying the short TTL, then change the address, and raise the TTL again once the move is done. On the client side, check that nothing pins answers forever: networkaddress.cache.ttl=-1 in a JVM, or a connection pool without a maximum lifetime, defeats any TTL.

compare.title: Asking the authority and asking a resolver

a.label: The authoritative server
a.title: dig @10.10.1.2 ledger.pay.test A +norecurse
a.html:
;; flags: qr aa; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 1, AUTHORITY: 0, ADDITIONAL: 0

;; ANSWER SECTION:
ledger.pay.test.	30	IN	A	10.10.4.40

the TTL is always the full 30: this is the original

b.label: The caching resolver
b.title: dig @10.10.1.20 ledger.pay.test A, twice
b.html:
;; flags: qr rd ra; QUERY: 1, ANSWER: 1, AUTHORITY: 0, ADDITIONAL: 0

;; ANSWER SECTION:
ledger.pay.test.	30	IN	A	10.10.4.40      first ask: fetched just now
ledger.pay.test.	24	IN	A	10.10.4.40      5 s later: a copy, 24 s left

compare.note: Both come from the lab network with env/net/dns.py running. The flags tell you which kind of answer you have: aa means the owner of the zone answered; ra without aa means a resolver passed on a copy, and its TTL is whatever is left of that copy's life. When you debug a DNS change, ask the authoritative server directly (dig +norecurse @ one of the zone's NS servers) to see the truth, and the resolver to see what your services see.

worked.title: Read a DNS answer by hand

steps.say: Take the answer frame from the third Try it. The DNS message starts at byte 42 (0x2a), after 14 bytes of Ethernet, 20 of IP and 8 of UDP. Its first 12 bytes are the header.
steps.code:
0x0020:  0002 0035 b83e 0045 6923 9984 8180 0001
0x0030:  0002 0000 0000 ...

99 84   ID 39300, the same as in the query
81 80   1000 0001 1000 0000: QR=1 (response), RD=1, RA=1, rcode 0 (NOERROR)
00 01   1 question     00 02   2 answers
00 00   0 authority    00 00   0 additional

steps.say: The question follows at offset 12 of the message: the name as labels, then type and class. It ends at offset 29.
steps.code:
07 65 78 61 6d 70 6c 65   length 7: "example"
03 63 6f 6d               length 3: "com"
00                        the root: end of the name
00 01   type A    00 01   class IN

steps.say: The first answer record starts at offset 29. Its name is a pointer: c0 has the top two bits set, and the remaining 14 bits, 00 0c, are offset 12, where example.com already appeared.
steps.code:
c0 0c         pointer to offset 12: "example.com"
00 01         type A
00 01         class IN
00 00 00 1e   TTL 30 seconds
00 04         4 bytes of data
ac 42 93 f3   172.66.147.243

steps.say: The second record has the same shape, with the other address. Add it all up: 12 bytes of header, 17 of question (13 of name, 4 of type and class) and 16 per record. Without compression each record would carry the 13-byte name instead of a 2-byte pointer.

lab.title: A DNS message codec and a resolver cache
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder. All 18 fail. DnsMessage.kt is finished: the header flags, questions and records as data classes, with each record's data already split by type. The tests read four real frames from src/test/resources/sfz/net/l09/: the query and answer from the third Try it, a CNAME answer and an NXDOMAIN.
In DnsCodec.kt, write encodeName and encodeQuery. The test compares your query with dig's, byte for byte.
Write readName: labels until the zero byte, following pointers, and only backwards. Then decode: header, questions, then the three record lists, each record's data decoded by type.

In ResolverCache.kt, write put and get with the rules from the fourth section: the smallest TTL for an answer, min(SOA TTL, SOA minimum) for a "no", nothing for errors. ResolverCacheTest moves a ManualClock instead of sleeping. Run the tests until all 18 pass.
hints: ByteBuffer.allocate(n).putShort(id.toShort())...array() builds the query. 12 bytes of header + the encoded name + 4.
In readName, remember where the name ended in the place you started: the first pointer you meet ends it 2 bytes after the pointer. Keep that, however many jumps follow.
A pointer is ((len and 0x3f) shl 8) or nextByte. Check target < at before you jump; that one check stops every loop.

Read TTLs and SOA numbers as unsigned: getInt(at).toLong() and 0xFFFF_FFFFL. After decoding a record's data, move on by RDLENGTH, not by what you read: a compressed name inside the data is shorter than the name it stands for.
In the cache, key on name.lowercase() and the type. Store the absolute expiry, clock() + seconds * 1000; get divides what is left by 1000 for whole seconds.

drill.title: Write readName from memory
drill.prompt: Without looking, write readName(msg: ByteArray, offset: Int): Pair<String, Int>: read a possibly compressed DNS name starting at offset, and return it with the offset just after the name where you started. Follow pointers, and refuse any pointer that doesn't point backwards. Then say in one sentence why the returned offset isn't simply where the last label ended.

answer.html: fun readName(msg: ByteArray, offset: Int): Pair<String, Int> { val labels = mutableListOf<String>() var at = offset var end = -1 // end of the name where we started while (true) { val len = msg[at].toInt() and 0xff when { len == 0 -> { // the root: done if (end < 0) end = at + 1 return labels.joinToString(".") to end } len and 0xc0 == 0xc0 -> { // compression pointer val target = ((len and 0x3f) shl 8) or (msg[at + 1].toInt() and 0xff) require(target < at) { "pointer at $at does not point backwards" } if (end < 0) end = at + 2 // the pointer is the last 2 bytes here at = target } else -> { // an ordinary label labels += String(msg, at + 1, len, Charsets.US_ASCII) at += 1 + len } } } } // After a pointer the rest of the name lives elsewhere in the message, so the next field // starts 2 bytes after the first pointer, not after the last label read.

recap: Names form a tree of zones. Each zone delegates its children with NS records, and only a zone's authoritative servers hold originals. The root knows only who runs each TLD.
Your stub resolver asks one recursive resolver (RD set); the resolver walks root, TLD and authoritative servers with iterative queries, following referrals and glue, and caches everything.
A DNS message is a 12-byte header (ID, flags, four counts), the question, then answer, authority and additional records. Names are length-prefixed labels, and c0 0c points back to offset 12.
Every copy lives for its TTL and nothing is pushed: "propagation" is caches expiring. NXDOMAIN is cached for min(SOA TTL, SOA minimum).
The JVM caches lookups for 30 s (failures 10 s) whatever the TTL, and pooled connections keep the address they opened with. Lower TTLs before a move, and give pools a maximum lifetime.

explain.prompt: The card issuer's ops team says: "We changed api.issuer.example to the new address an hour ago, DNS has propagated, why are you still calling the old one?" Explain what happens between their authoritative server and your Quarkus service, which caches are involved, and what you would check and change.
explain.answer: Nothing in DNS propagates. Their authoritative server answered with the new address the moment they changed it, but every resolver that cached the old record keeps its copy until its TTL runs out, so if the old TTL was a day, our company resolver can be serving the old address for up to a day after the change. On our side there are two more copies. The JVM caches every lookup for 30 seconds by default, which only adds a little. The bigger one is our HTTP connection pool: DNS is only consulted when a connection opens, so pooled connections opened before the change keep going to the old address until the pool closes them. I'd check what our resolver returns and the TTL it shows, compare with dig +norecurse against their authoritative servers, and look at our pool's maximum connection lifetime. Next time I'd ask them to lower the TTL to a minute a day before the move, and we'd make sure the pool recycles connections within a few minutes.

deeper.html:
DNSSEC. Run dig +trace without +nodnssec and you see DS and RRSIG records at every step. With DNSSEC each zone signs its records, and the parent vouches for the child's key with a DS record, a chain of trust up to the root's key built into validating resolvers. It proves an answer came from the zone's owner and wasn't changed. It doesn't encrypt anything: anyone on the path can still read which names you ask for.

Encrypted DNS. DNS over TLS (RFC 7858, port 853), over HTTPS (RFC 8484) and over QUIC (RFC 9250) encrypt the hop between a client and its resolver, so the network in between can't read or change the questions. Browsers often use DoH directly. Your JVM services still use the operating system's plain UDP stub unless the host runs a local resolver that forwards over TLS.

Bigger answers. RFC 1035 capped UDP answers at 512 bytes. EDNS (the extra record +noedns switched off) lets a client announce a bigger buffer; since DNS Flag Day 2020 resolvers use 1,232 bytes so answers fit an IPv6 packet without fragments, and anything bigger is truncated (TC flag) and asked again over TCP. A firewall that blocks TCP port 53 therefore breaks only big answers, which makes it hard to spot.

ndots in Kubernetes. A pod's /etc/resolv.conf usually says options ndots:5 plus several search domains. A name with fewer than five dots, such as api.issuer.example, is first tried with each search domain appended (api.issuer.example.default.svc.cluster.local and so on), so one lookup can become several queries and several NXDOMAINs. A trailing dot (api.issuer.example.) or a lower ndots avoids it.

Not every "no" is NXDOMAIN. Some DNS providers answer a query for a name that doesn't exist with NOERROR and no records instead of NXDOMAIN; example.com's servers did that for nosuchhost-4242.example.com while this lesson was written. Resolvers cache both kinds of "no" the same way, by the SOA.
